nodes.label: How much of the reaction is the perceiver?
How much do situations change the perceiver's contribution?
Are perceiver effects stable across stimulus sets?
Study 1 — variance decomposition of first impressions
nodes.description: Round-robin ratings: 312 perceivers crossed with 240 faces, every perceiver rating every face. Variance split into perceiver, target and residual with a cross-classified random-effects model; 95% intervals from a group-resampled bootstrap.
nodes.result: The perceiver accounts for 34% of reaction variance — ICC(perceiver) = .34, 95% CI [.29, .39]. The target accounts for 21%. Roughly a third of a first impression is the person doing the impressing.

nodes.label: Does the perceiver effect depend on the situation?
nodes.description: Situation × perceiver interaction term added to the Study 1 model, with a permutation null over situation labels within perceiver (B = 2,000).
nodes.result: Null, with a bound: p = .665, and the design could have detected an interaction of d = 0.10 at 80% power. Write this as a limit on what was visible, not as an absence.

nodes.label: Study 2 — cross-stimulus replication
nodes.description: The same decomposition on a second, independent face set, to see whether the perceiver share travels. Data collection is in progress; the holdout estimate stays sealed until wave-2 coding is frozen.

nodes.label: Mischel & Shoda (1995) — A cognitive-affective system theory of personality
Write the nulls as limits on what was visible, not as absences — a reviewer reads a null as a claim of absence unless the sentence blocks it.
